title: HTML colors: legacy attributes and modern CSS
learningObjectives: Explain html colors: legacy attributes and modern css and its role in modern HTML.
Select the correct elements, attributes, APIs, or browser behaviour for a practical use case.
Distinguish current practices from obsolete, limited, or legacy techniques.
Build and inspect a working example while considering accessibility and maintainability.
Diagnose common implementation errors and explain the trade-offs of the chosen approach.

understand.concept: HTML content and CSS presentation are separate responsibilities. Older HTML tutorials demonstrate named colours, hexadecimal RGB notation, and RGB values through presentational attributes such as bgcolor. Those attributes are obsolete for modern authoring. Use CSS color, background-color, border-color, and related properties instead. Hex uses #RRGGBB (optionally #RGB); rgb() expresses red, green, and blue channels; modern color functions can also express alpha. A colour value is not meaningful without considering contrast, state, and the element it styles.
understand.whyItMatters: This topic preserves historical W3Schools coverage while teaching the modern boundary: HTML describes meaning and CSS controls appearance. Learners should be able to read old examples without copying obsolete patterns into new work.
understand.analogy: HTML identifies what a room contains; CSS chooses the paint and lighting.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not explain the cascade, inheritance, colour spaces, transparency compositing, or accessibility contrast requirements.

explain.narrative: Compare an obsolete bgcolor attribute with a CSS rule. Then inspect equivalent named, hexadecimal, and RGB colour values and choose a foreground/background pair that remains readable.

examples.code: Named and hexadecimal colours
examples.explanation: The paragraph uses a named text colour and a six-digit hexadecimal background. Inline style is shown only for a compact demonstration; production styles normally belong in a stylesheet.
examples.expectedOutput: A navy paragraph on a pale blue background.

examples.code: RGB and HEX in CSS
examples.explanation: The class rule keeps presentation outside the HTML content. Modern space-separated RGB syntax is supported by current browsers; use a project compatibility policy when targeting older browsers.
examples.expectedOutput: A bordered notice with dark blue text and a pale blue background.

practise.guidedTask: Replace a legacy bgcolor attribute in a supplied page with a class and stylesheet rule. Create the same colour using a named colour, HEX, and RGB; compare the results and check text contrast.
practise.independentTask: Build a small theme with primary, surface, text, and border colours. Document why the chosen combinations are readable and ensure colour is not the only way to communicate status.
hints: Do not use obsolete HTML colour attributes in new documents.
Keep colour declarations in CSS, preferably in a reusable class or custom property.
Check text and non-text contrast; colour alone must not carry essential meaning.

questions.prompt: Which language should control modern page colours?
questions.explanation: CSS controls presentation; HTML should express document structure and meaning.
The six hexadecimal digits encode red, green, and blue channels.

questions.prompt: Why should new pages avoid bgcolor on body or table elements?
options: It is an obsolete presentational HTML attribute
It is required for responsive design
questions.answer: It is an obsolete presentational HTML attribute
questions.explanation: Modern presentation belongs in CSS rather than obsolete presentational attributes.

questions.prompt: Which is a valid CSS colour declaration?
questions.explanation: CSS declarations use a property, colon, value, and terminating semicolon.

questions.prompt: What should be checked after choosing foreground and background colours?
options: Contrast and whether meaning is conveyed without colour alone
Only whether the colours look fashionable
Whether every element uses a different colour
questions.answer: Contrast and whether meaning is conveyed without colour alone
questions.explanation: Accessible colour use requires readable contrast and additional non-colour cues where needed.
